name: Daria Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. So you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work out of the Millbrook depot, which covers the farms and villages north of town. Distribution lines, so wooden poles, transformers, the wires that run down the lanes to people's houses. Most days it's planned work, changing old poles or crossarms, and then when a storm comes through it's anything and everything until the lights are back. I've done this for thirty-one years and I still like the moment a whole village comes back on at once.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The tablet. Two years ago they gave every truck a tablet for job tickets and photos and sign-offs. I don't touch it. My partner on the truck, Kofi, does it, and I buy his coffee in return. That's been our deal and it works fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said about the tablet: lots of fuss, then it's just another thing in the truck. People get excited, then they get bored. Online I don't say anything, I'm not on there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I get to finish the way I planned. Four more years, out at sixty-two, when the pension pays in full. Raúl and I have the flat we rent out, the savings are fine, so nothing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing, really. I'd keep going on the trucks, keep buying Kofi his coffee, and keep putting money aside like we do every month. Maybe I'd look at the pension letter one more time and tick off the months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a forecast that says rain and then it's just a bit cloudy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So the tablet stays, but nothing bigger. Does that suit you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It suits me fine. I don't need the world to change. I need my knees to last four more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Kofi talk about in the truck if this happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Football, probably, and his wedding. He's getting married in the spring. We'd laugh about it, the robots that never came.

S0.say: It's lots of fuss, and then it's just another thing in the truck. People get excited, then they get bored.
S0.think: It means I get to finish the way I planned, out at sixty-two on a full pension. Between the rental flat and our savings, nothing changes for us.
S0.do: Keeps working on the trucks as normal and keeps saving every month. Leaves the tablet to her truck partner and counts down to retiring at sixty-two.
S0.quote: I don't need the world to change. I need my knees to last four more years.
S0.fieldNote: Daria has a plan and a date, and this scenario leaves both alone. She avoids technology by trading coffee with her younger partner, which says a lot about how she handles change. She's not anxious, just settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it'll be like the tablet but bigger, and we'll all moan about it and then get on with it. At work I'd probably keep quiet and see what they actually bring in. I'm not one for big speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it means more screens and more checking. More things that want my login. The poles still need climbing and the transformers still need changing, so I don't think they'll get rid of me. But I'd feel pushed, and I don't like being pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what the company brings in. Let the young ones try it first. If it gets to be too much, I'd talk to Raúl about going at sixty-one instead of sixty-two, even with a smaller pension, but I wouldn't decide that in the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when they change the route of a job and nobody tells you why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes in your own day, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the fault-finding. Now, when a line trips, we drive out and look. They'd have some program that tells you exactly which pole. That'd save fuel, I'll give them that. But then they'd want me to read the program, and that's where I'd be stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let the young ones go first. What if the company makes it mandatory?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd learn the minimum, the way I did with the radio codes years ago. I'd hate it. I'd make Kofi show me three times and write it on a card in my pocket. I'm not proud, I just don't like it.

S1.say: It'll be like the tablet but bigger. We'll all moan about it and then get on with it.
S1.think: I think it means more screens and more logins, though the poles still need climbing, so they won't get rid of me. But I'd feel pushed, and I don't like being pushed.
S1.do: Waits to see what the company introduces and lets younger crew members try it first. Learns only the minimum if forced, and considers retiring a year earlier at sixty-one if it gets too much, without deciding in the first year.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like having a job changed without being told why.
S1.quote: I'd make Kofi show me three times and write it on a card in my pocket. I'm not proud, I just don't like it.
S1.fieldNote: Her worry isn't losing the job but being made to change how she does it. She's honest that she would hate learning new software, without being defensive about it. Retiring a year early is her safety valve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say they're dreaming, at first. Then if it really came, I'd say well, that's that, and I'd ask the company what they're offering. I'm not going to march about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a robot can climb a pole by 2028, I'm sixty and they don't need me. I'm fine for money, that's not it. It's that I'd be leaving two years short, on someone else's terms, and I've always left things on my own terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to the pension office and get the real number for going at sixty. I'd stop the holiday we were planning and put that money aside too, just in case the rental flat goes empty or the pension changes. And if they offered a package, I'd take it and not look back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not scared for food on the table, more like the floor tilted and I don't know which way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years puts you at sixty. What does that do to your pension plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It takes a cut off it, maybe a fifth. We could live with that. Raúl's pension, the rent from the flat, our savings. I've done the sums in my head more than once. It's not poverty, it's just less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Raúl that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, you got your wish, I'm home. He's been saying I should stop since he retired. Then I'd probably go out and sit in the garden for a while by myself.

S2.say: They're dreaming, at first. If it really came, I'd say that's that and ask the company what they're offering, but I'm not going to march about it.
S2.think: I'm fine for money, that's not it. It's that I'd be leaving two years short, on someone else's terms, and I've always left things on my own terms.
S2.do: Gets the exact pension figure for retiring at sixty from the pension office straight away. Cancels a planned holiday and puts the money aside, and takes any redundancy package the company offers.
S2.feel: Anxious, like the floor has tilted, though not afraid for money.
S2.quote: Not scared for food on the table, more like the floor tilted and I don't know which way.
S2.fieldNote: Money isn't the issue for her; control is. She's done the sums and knows a smaller pension would be enough. The image of her sitting alone in the garden was the quiet emotional centre of the interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see. Five years is a long time, they said the tablet would change everything too. I'd keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031 I'm sixty-three. I'd planned to go at sixty-two. So really, it comes after me. I feel for the young ones, but for me it's about the same as nothing happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as planned and retire at sixty-two. Keep saving the same each month. Maybe I'd tell Kofi to start thinking about what he does next, because he's thirty and he'll be the one it lands on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only a little. It's like weather coming in after you've already packed up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is this different for you from AGI by 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the difference between them pushing me and me just leaving. With two years, I'm shown the door. With five, I'm already gone by the time it gets here. I'd sleep fine with five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use those years to learn anything new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know that sounds stubborn. But why would I learn to work with a robot for one year? I'd rather spend that time on the trucks doing what I know, and let the people with thirty years left do the learning.

S3.say: We'll see. Five years is a long time, and they said the tablet would change everything too. I'd keep my head down and get on with the job.
S3.think: By 2031 I'm sixty-three and I'd planned to go at sixty-two, so it comes after me. I feel for the young ones, but for me it's about the same as nothing happening.
S3.do: Carries on as planned and retires at sixty-two, saving the same amount each month. Encourages her younger truck partner to start thinking about what he'll do next.
S3.feel: Slightly uneasy, but mostly relieved that it arrives after she's gone.
S3.quote: With two years, I'm shown the door. With five, I'm already gone by the time it gets here.
S3.fieldNote: The timing does almost all the work for her: five years means it arrives after her planned exit. She refuses to learn anything new for one year of use, and she knows how that sounds. Her concern turns briefly to Kofi.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck to them. Ten years is plenty of time to sort it out. That's for the next lot to deal with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing for me, really. I'm retired by then, in the garden, maybe with grandchildren if Pilar gets on with it. I'd just hope the lights still come on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Retire at sixty-two, as planned, and hand over my climbing gear. I'd keep the savings where they are and let the rent from the flat top up the pensions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's somebody else's storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you be by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the garden, or driving Raúl mad. Probably taking Pilar's kids to school, if there are any. Not thinking about poles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about it worry you, even though you're retired?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, about who fixes things when they go wrong. If the robot's on the pole and the robot breaks in a storm, who goes up? I'd like to think there'd still be a Kofi somewhere.

S4.say: Good luck to them, ten years is plenty of time to sort it out. That's for the next lot to deal with.
S4.think: It means nothing for me, really, because I'm retired by then. I'd just hope the lights still come on.
S4.do: Retires at sixty-two as planned and hands over her climbing gear. Leaves the savings where they are and relies on rent from the flat to top up the pensions.
S4.feel: Calm, as if it's someone else's problem.
S4.quote: If the robot's on the pole and the robot breaks in a storm, who goes up?
S4.fieldNote: She is completely untouched by this version and says so. Even so, her practical sense surfaces: someone still has to fix the fixer. A pragmatic, quietly stubborn person who has arranged her life to avoid surprises.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, 2028. Not because I'd go hungry, but because I'd be pushed out two years early. What would help is the company being straight with people my age. Tell us the package early and give us the full pension if they're the ones ending it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked about the storms. Whatever happens with computers, when a tree comes down on a line at two in the morning, somebody has to get in the truck. I've been that somebody for thirty-one years. I'd like that to count for something.

headlineQuote: I've done this for thirty-one years and I still like the moment a whole village comes back on at once.
portrait: Daria Diaz is a 58-year-old distribution lineworker at a rural depot who has spent thirty-one years on wooden poles and storm call-outs. She avoids technology so firmly that she trades coffee with her younger truck partner so he'll handle the job tablet. With savings, a rental flat and a plan to retire at sixty-two, she is calm when AI stalls or arrives after she's gone. Steady disruption makes her uneasy because she'd be pushed to change, and AGI by 2028 makes her anxious, less for money than for losing control of how and when she leaves. She is pragmatic, private and quietly stubborn.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd be pushed out two years before her planned retirement.
whatWouldHelp: The company being straight with older workers, telling them about packages early and paying a full pension if the company is the one ending their job.
